Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with golden hills, far mountains, and one big tree on the right hill.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

12 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The striped balloon, envelope centered 28% across and 15% down (frame). Light: The setting sun, low and a little left of center (43% across, 41% down): the balloon is lit on its right side, the tree on its left side.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: cloud bodies and undersidesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: dabbing patches on the slopesOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #8 round: the trunkRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • old stiff flat or round: dabbing the crownOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #10 round or old stiff flat: bigger dabs on the front rowsOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #4 round: the outline and stripe linesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the ropesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

STEP 1 OF 12

Paint the sunset sky and the sun

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and a little left of center; every highlight goes on the side facing it.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Sky blue, paint the top 8% in long side-to-side strokes.
  3. Wipe the brush and blend down while wet, as in the values table, to a straight edge 56% down. Work fast; keep the right side a little redder.
  4. Dab the sun with the #6 round: centered 37% across, 41% down, about 5% wide. Soften its edge with small circles.
  5. Done: a smooth blue-to-gold sky with a pale sun; everything below 56% is still white.
Build the depth, dark first
ValuePaintWhere

  • Sky blue new3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, a touch of yellow, a touch of burnt sienna
  • Sunset gold new3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 2 parts white
  • Pale sun yellow new4 parts white, 1 part yellow, a touch of red

Mix plenty of Sunset gold; you'll want the same color for the whole lower sky.

Brushes

1 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat across the whole width in one stroke, then stroke back over the join between blue and gold while it's wet.

Small circles. Circle the round's tip around the sun's edge so it melts into the gold.

Watch out: Don't stop the gold at the mountain line; run it down to 56% so the hills go over sky, not white canvas.

Watch out: Colors dry a little darker: test each mix on the palette edge before a big area.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 12

Paint the big soft clouds

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the 3/4 inch flat and creamy Coral cloud, make small circles for three masses where the picture shows them.
  3. Left: 0 to 20% across, 15% to 33% down. Middle: 30% to 70% across, 12% to 37% down. Upper right: 55% across to the edge, top to 30% down.
  4. With the flat on its edge, pull a few long thin Coral cloud streaks low across 5% to 60% across, 25% to 38% down, sky showing between.
  5. Shade and light each cloud as in the values table.
  6. Done: bumpy coral clouds with blue sky between them at the top; the sun stays clear.

Brushes

3/4 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

Small circles with the brush tip. Circle the corner of the flat to build each bumpy top; keep the bottoms flatter.

Dry brush. Wipe the gold off until almost none is left, then skim it along the bottom edges nearest the sun.

Watch out: Leave blue gaps between the clouds near the top; don't cover the whole sky.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 12

Paint the far mountains

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the 3/4 inch flat and creamy Mountain violet, paint the range in horizontal strokes.
  3. Peaks: 2% across at 37% down, and 59% across at 40% down. It dips just below the sun and ends 44% down at the right edge.
  4. Fill down to 56% down.
  5. Add the Ridge blue ridge along 45% to 52% down, softer edges than the peaks.
  6. Done: two flat blue layers, sun fully above them.

Watch out: Don't paint into the sun's bottom edge.

STEP 4 OF 12

Paint the golden hills

  1. Let the mountains dry.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Hill gold, paint the left hilltop: 50% down at the left edge, dipping to 57% at 40% across.
  3. Then the right hilltop, rising from 60% down at 25% across to 46% at 85% across.
  4. Add Hill olive lower on each hill, blending wet into the gold with sloping strokes, down to a straight edge at 66%.
  5. Let it dry. With an old stiff flat and Hill olive, dab short sloping patches on the lower slopes, then a few Hill gold dabs on the tops.
  6. Done: smooth gold-and-olive hills; below 66% still white.

Brushes

1 inch flatold stiff flat

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Stroke along each hill's slope, not straight across, so the hills look rounded.

Wet-on-wet blend. Lay the olive into the wet gold and stroke the join a few times; stop when it drags.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat with a little paint in short sloping patches, following the hill.

Watch out: Stopping the hills at the lavender line; run them to 66% so the lavender goes over them.

Watch out: Keep the dabs loose and few; the hills are still far away.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 12

Paint the big tree

  1. Let the hills dry.
  2. Trunk: with the #8 round and creamy Trunk brown, press and lift upward from its base on the hilltop (86% across, 46% down) to 40% down, a short fork at the top. Build it as in the diagram.
  3. Crown: dab the oval of overlapping clumps, 74% to 99% across and 22% to 43% down, in the values table's order.
  4. Done: a leafy round crown, darker on the right.

Brushes

#8 roundold stiff flat or round

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round's belly at the base and lift as you pull up, so the trunk tapers.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush straight down with little paint; overlap the taps into clumps.

Watch out: Smooth crown edges; keep dabbing so the outline stays leafy.

Watch out: Try a few dabs on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 12

Lay in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Let the hills dry.
  2. Dot the point where the rows meet: 58% across, 62% down.
  3. With the #6 round and creamy Path orange, pull the two paths from the dot: the left to 29% to 37% across at the bottom edge, the right to 74% to 84%.
  4. With the 1 inch flat, fill the rows in Lavender mid with strokes toward the dot, as in the diagram. Once dry, pull a thin Lavender dark furrow between rows.
  5. Done: flat dark rows and two orange paths; no white anywhere.

Brushes

1 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Start each stroke at the front and pull it toward the dot, wide in front and thin near it.

Watch out: Rows that don't point at the dot; check a few with the brush handle held from it.

Watch out: It may look plain and dark now. That's the ugly stage, and it's normal.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why this tool: The rows before any texture; no filter can strip the dabs off the finish. Redone once so the paths line up with the dabbed rows painted over them.

Why a diagram: Placing rows in perspective takes more than a sentence: every row and both paths point to one spot.

STEP 7 OF 12

Dab the back lavender rows

  1. Let the rows dry.
  2. With the #6 round and creamy Lavender mid, dab short upright marks along each back row, from 62% down to about 80% down.
  3. Make them smallest near the top, a little bigger lower down, with dark gaps between. Add white to the mix for a few dabs on each row's top.
  4. Done: the back rows look bumpy; the front rows below 80% are still flat.

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Touch the tip down and lift with a little flick up, so each dab is taller than wide.

Watch out: Covering the dark base completely; it's the shadow between the flowers.

Watch out: Try a few dabs on scrap paper first.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: The back-rows pass ends in a straight line at about 80% down, with flat bands below it; the boundary is a pass edge, not a row edge. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 10 OF 12

Paint the balloon's stripes

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #4 round, outline the balloon as in the diagram: 11% to 29% across, 3.5% to 27% down, widest 14% down.
  3. Draw curved stripe lines from top to band; fill each with creamy color, left to right: red, blue, red, yellow, blue, red, yellow, teal, orange, a yellow sliver.
  4. Brown band at 26% to 28% down.
  5. Done: flat stripes, no shading.

Brushes

#4 roundLiner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Dry brush. Wipe the brush nearly clean and skim it down the stripes so the light looks soft.

Liner work. Paint thinned to ink, brush upright, one light steady pull per rope.

Watch out: Thick ropes; thin the paint and keep the liner upright.

Watch out: Practise a liner line on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A striped hot air balloon over a lavender field at sunset

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, text, borders, or screen edges.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: the left 11% (clouds and part of the village) and the right 4% of sky and hill

Why: The picture is 3:2 and the canvas 14:11; the balloon, sun, and tree all fit a crop, so no render was needed.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, a village of houses, cypress trees, scattered bushes, a lake glint. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, every lavender stalk. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined clouds. More than 8 parts: yes, with the village and bushes.

Changed: Dropped the village, cypresses, small bushes, and lake. Merged the clouds into four or five big masses, the mountains into two layers, the fields into smooth bands. Turned the lavender into rows of loose dabs, the tree crown into dabbed clumps.

Why: The original had the exact clutter that broke the earlier balloon lesson; with it gone every part is one big shape or one repeated mark.

A bright sunset over a lavender field with a striped balloon high on the left and a lone tree on the right hill. The balloon is the focal point and the hardest shape; the lavender is the biggest area and the biggest risk, because thousands of stalks can't be a beginner step. The lesson is about a glowing sky, simple layered land, rows that lead to one point, and a round striped balloon.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with golden hills, far mountains, and one big tree on the right hill.
Focal point: The striped balloon, envelope centered 28% across and 15% down (frame).
Light: The setting sun, low and a little left of center (43% across, 41% down): the balloon is lit on its right side, the tree on its left side.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky with the sun
  2. big soft clouds
  3. far blue-violet mountains
  4. golden rolling hills
  5. the big tree on the right hill
  6. lavender rows and dirt paths
  7. the striped hot air balloon
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named acrylic-paint-along-beginner.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along back to front fits a landscape with a clear far-to-near order (sky, mountains, hills, tree, lavender) and one subject painted on top.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

The owner named paint-along; a toned ground and sketch would also hide the sunset glow that comes from painting on white.

How the paint recipes were worked out24 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order12 steps

Back to front: sky with the sun, clouds over it, far mountains, hills, the tree on the hill, then the lavender in three passes (flat rows, mid dabs back then front, light tips), and the balloon last as the subject, in base, shading, and highlight steps.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky and the sun

    Everything else sits on the sky, and the sun belongs in the wet gradient, so they go together first.

  2. 2. Paint the big soft clouds

    Clouds sit on the sky and need it dry; three values make them round.

  3. 3. Paint the far mountains

    Farthest land, flat and cool, before anything in front of it.

  4. 4. Paint the golden hills

    The middle ground, painted down past where the lavender starts.

  5. 5. Paint the big tree

    Stands on the hill and in front of the sky, so it comes after both.

  6. 6. Lay in the lavender rows and paths

    The near field's base: rows and paths set the perspective before any texture.

  7. 7. Dab the back lavender rows

    First texture pass, back rows only, so no step jumps from flat rows to a full field of dabs.

  8. 8. Dab the front lavender rows

    Second half of the same pass, bigger marks in front.

  9. 9. Add the light lavender tips

    Light over the dark dabs, last for the field.

  10. 10. Paint the balloon's stripes

    The subject goes on last over the dry sky; flat stripes first.

  11. 11. Shade the balloon

    A teacher's separate shading layer makes the balloon round.

  12. 12. Highlight the balloon and hang the basket

    The brightest highlights and the small details (ropes, basket) end the painting.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three steps build a shape a beginner can't start from the picture alone: the tree, the converging lavender rows, and the balloon; each got a diagram. The rest are fills or repeated marks.

  • Step 5: Paint the big tree beginner check

    Noticed: A whole tree appears in one step, and where the trunk forks into the crown isn't clear from the picture.

    Pieces: A trunk pulled up to a short fork, then four overlapping clumps for the crown, then light dabs on the sun side, the way a tree is drawn as trunk plus masses.

  • Step 6: Lay in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: Placing rows in perspective takes more than a sentence: every row and both paths point to one spot.

    Pieces: A dot first, then the two paths fanning from it, then row lines from the edges toward the dot.

  • Step 10: Paint the balloon's stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The subject appears whole, and its stripes must curve with the shape.

    Pieces: A circle for the top, a taper down to the brown band, then curved stripe lines that meet at the top and the band.

A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • lock-steps keeps the first raw render in trials/raw/ and doesn't refresh it when render-step redoes a step after a lock; the redo is silently overwritten by the stale raw on the next lock. I copied the redo into trials/raw/ by hand. render-step (or lock) should update the raw copy.
  • Splitting a too-dense texture step into back and front passes can be done for free by giving one render two steps with different lock regions, but the pass boundary is a straight line across the rows unless the region follows a row.
  • Ran the first lock before review round 2 so the reviewer saw the locked images; the round 1 cloud issue (sky edge moved up) was fixed by the lock, not a redo.
  • The research notes have no direct guidance for lavender or other row crops beyond strokes toward a vanishing point; I used that stroke plus dabbing in passes.
  • Plan step ids and the NN_ file names are tied by position, so inserting a step means renaming every later image by hand.
